newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia's acting PM seen out to prove himself.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia's acting PM seen out to prove himself.

text.p: Taking a page from the master's book, Acting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim is acting like a man in a hurry.

In the three weeks since his boss, Mahathir Mohammad, left on an extended trip abroad, Anwar has launched an anti-corruption campaign that has seen six politicians lose their jobs, announced a minor cabinet reshuffle, and has dominated local news headlines.

He presided at a cabinet meeting last week that took away the national news agency Bernama's exclusive right to distribute foreign news, a move to promote the free flow of information in the country, officials said.

A key friend and ally, Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, chairman of the youth wing of the ruling United Malays National Organisation (UMNO), was dispatched to Singapore to help patch up a nasty row between the two countries.
To top it off, the ruling National Front won three by-elections at the end of May with Anwar leading the campaign.
The boss could not have asked for anything better.
"He's certainly busy but some of the things appear to have been made before Mahathir left," said political analyst Rustam Sani.
"While he appears to be acting on his own, he also appears to be working in concert, or at least with the consent of the real prime minister."
Tongues wagged when Mahathir announced he was taking two months leave abroad -- a mix of holidays, official business and perhaps a stab at writing a memoir.
Mahathir works killer schedules that would exhaust others half his age as he builds the industrialised nation of his "Vision 2020" dream.
Was the 71-year-old leader ill?
Was Anwar being tested for the top job, or being given on-the-job training? Or, for the conspiracy theorists, was the Machiavellian Mahathir giving his deputy enough rope to hang himself?

The youthful-looking Mahathir had a quintuple heart by-pass in 1989, but seems remarkably fit for a man his age. He didn't put a deputy in charge when recuperating for almost three months after that operation.
Mahathir sightings abroad have dispelled rumours in diplomatic circles that he may have gone overseas for cardiovascular care.
The prime minister was spotted walking by Hyde Park on a shopping expedition. An avid horseman, he reportedly took a side trip to Argentina visiting a ranch owned by a Malaysian businessmen.
Last weekend he was in Turkey for a summit of eight developing countries and this week he is in Lebanon for an official visit.
What surprised everyone, including Anwar, was that Mahathir formally transferred the powers of the prime minister and, perhaps more importantly, the UMNO presidency to his deputy before he went.
Anwar has said the formal transfer of powers, announced at a cabinet meeting, was not necessary as the Constitution already provides for the deputy to act in the prime minister's absence.
Mahathir, who has a history of uneasy relationships with his deputies since becoming premier in 1981, had not formally named an acting prime minister in a dozen years.
But he has often seemed to be a man in a hurry to see a slew of major infrastructure projects completed by 1999, when many think he'll retire, though few would bet big money on it.
Anwar appears to be relishing his moment in the sun.
Already the finance minister, he has taken over Mahathir's coveted portfolio as home minister as well, giving him almost unprecedented powers.
Mahathir, a former doctor, has focused the 16 years of his administration on industrialising the Malaysian economy.

High up on the agenda of Anwar, a former philosophy major and Islamic student leader, are themes dubbed the "Asian Renaissance", the "Just and Caring Society" and the "Perfection of the Malaysian Man."

Where Mahathir has defined himself by pet projects such as a national car and a zone for global information technology companies, Anwar frequently campaigns for low cost housing and anti-poverty programmes.
Last week, Anwar launched a multi-million ringgit fund to improve the livelihood of poor fishermen.
The test appears to be about how tough Anwar really is, analysts say. Can he stand up to the powerful in UMNO, make the hard calls and talk tough to the West?
Anwar himself says that he and Mahathir do not differ in substance, just in style.

Chatting to visitors in his office recently, Anwar referred to his speech to an Asian Development Bank meeting in Japan last month when he urged the bank not to bow to pressure from the West for stricter loan conditionalities.
"I was tough. I didn't want to give him any excuse not to go ahead with the acting PM," Anwar quipped.
